blocks.text: be a role model for your dog
What matters?
We are a team based on a combination of communication, trust, empathy and mutual respect.
Be present: concentrate fully on your dog when you are out together.
Pay attention to signals: learn to understand your dog's non-verbal communication (posture, deviations, body signals, breathing).
Offer security: show it through consistent leadership that it can rely on you.
Make it interesting: vary routes and activities in terms of territory and content.
Show appreciation: reward and praise generously and show it that you notice its efforts.
Our dog orients itself towards us. The way we are is the way our dog will be.
The mental connection during shared activities is a fundamental and indispensable building block.
Discover and train your mental tools.
Your mental tools
Understanding through calm and defined body language.
Understanding through a calm, peaceful and reliable voice.
Cultivate your empathy and train emotional synchronisation.
Empathise with your dog without constructing things intellectually.
Convey a clear distribution of roles through fair leadership and unconditional trust.
Train all layers of sensory perception for shared experience.
Never forget reward and motivation.
Pursue a common goal through teamwork.
Recognise the importance of routine and structure.
Be patient and mediating in all situations.

lessons.title: Mental training from a professional perspective

blocks.text: How your dog reacts to your mood

Dogs pay attention to the emotional expression of their humans. In one study (Müller et al., 2015), dogs learned to distinguish between friendly and angry human facial expressions, even in unfamiliar people.

In uncertain situations, dogs orient themselves towards their human. A study (Merola et al., 2012) showed that dogs treated an unfamiliar object differently depending on whether the owner gave a positive or a negative signal.
Your inner attitude affects the dog through facial expression, body tension, voice and movement. A calm and confident attitude gives it reliable orientation in uncertain situations.
Your mood is thus part of every situation in which you train with your dog. This makes looking after it a training task.
Presence: directing attention consciously
Dogs recognise whether their human is attentive. In experiments (Call et al., 2003), dogs directed their requests more clearly to people who were facing them and looking at them.
Anyone whose thoughts are elsewhere or who is looking at their phone sends the dog unclear signals. The dog then tends to look for orientation and occupation in the surroundings by itself.
Exercise: take one minute before every walk. Feel your feet on the ground, breathe out calmly and notice the sounds, smells and light in the surroundings.
Put your phone away or switch it to silent during your time together. Direct your attention to your dog and the surroundings.
The mood log
Before every walk, note your mood on a scale from 1 (very tense) to 5 (very calm).
After the walk, briefly note how your dog behaved: calm, excited, responsive, distracted.
Keep the log for at least two weeks under “My reflection” at the end of this page.
Then compare your mood with your dog's behaviour. You will see in which situations your tension is transferred to it, and can start there in a targeted way.
What mental training achieves and what it does not
A calm and clear inner attitude improves the conditions for any training.
It does not replace the step-by-step build-up of exercises, sufficient repetitions and a reliable reward.

In the case of conspicuous signs of unexplained fear, defensiveness or sudden, strong changes in behaviour, have possible physical causes checked by a vet and consider supportive guidance from very experienced dog trainers.

Sources: Müller C. A. et al. (2015): Dogs can discriminate emotional expressions of human faces. Current Biology 25 (5), 601–605. Merola I., Prato-Previde E., Marshall-Pescini S. (2012): Dogs' social referencing towards owners and strangers. PLoS ONE 7 (10). Call J. et al. (2003): Domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) are sensitive to the attentional state of humans. Journal of Comparative Psychology 117 (3), 257–263.
Practice impulse: the inner mirror

On your next walk, consciously pay attention to your inner basic mood. If your dog shows behaviour that is uncomfortable for you, pause and first check the state of your inner mental alignment. Collect yourself, breathe more calmly, smile inwardly, come to rest, in order to harmonise the energy of the situation. Only then walk on.
Your mental tools are the link between you, your dog, the environment and the course of the situation.
Without internalised mental tools, the risk of misunderstandings and faulty training increases.
Without good mental tools, everything is nothing. Training these tools takes time, depending on your personal individual condition.
Always be conscious when you are out with your dog.
